text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- The New England Patriots will be without starting guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown for Thursday's road game against the Chicago Bears due to injuries, coach Mike Vrabel said.

Vera-Tucker played every snap this season at left guard before injuring his hamstring in the second quarter of Sunday's win over the visiting New York Jets, his former team. Brown, meanwhile, was the third right guard to start -- after Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten both landed on injured reserve -- and he hobbled off in the second half of Sunday's game with a knee injury.

Vrabel said Walter Rouse, a three-year veteran acquired in a trade from the Minnesota Vikings on Aug. 30, will start at left guard. It will be his first career NFL start.

Vrabel said nine-year veteran Matt Pryor, whom the Patriots signed off the Arizona Cardinals' practice squad Oct. 1, will start at right guard. He has started 40 career games, with 15 of them coming in the 2024 season with the Bears.

Quarterback Drake Maye wasn't sacked in Sunday's win, and he credited the offensive line -- which also played without veteran right tackle Morgan Moses (foot) for two-plus quarters -- for exemplary work.

"I feel like it's been every week somebody stepping up," Maye said. "On the flip side of it, it's unfortunate seeing so many of our guys go down. I'm impressed with how the coaches have been handling it, of kind of moving personnel around and fixing things on the sideline and adjusting."

Moses was limited in practice in recent days, but Vrabel said he has a chance to play against the Bears.

There is little doubt the Chicago Bears have missed the presence of running back Kyle Monangai in their offense over the past two weeks, though the team sent mixed messages as to his potential availability against the New England Patriots on the upcoming edition of Thursday Night Football.

Monangai has been out the previous two contests due to a turf toe injury he suffered during a career game against the New York Jets in Week 4, in which he rushed the football 30 times for 146 yards and two scores.

The team designated him as a DNP (did not practice) for Monday’s walkthrough across all platforms. However, the Bears sent out conflicting information after Tuesday’s session as to Monangai’s status.

“So this is interesting,” Brendan Sugrue of USA Today’s Bears Wire posted to X Tuesday. “The injury report @BearsPR tweeted has Kyle Monangai as a DNP. But the Bears’ app and website list him as LP [limited participant]. Which one is correct? Credit to @tekster420 for pointing it out.”

Kyle Monangai Has Proven Vital to Bears’ Elite Run Game This Season

It is possible there was simply a miscommunication or an error somewhere within the organization as to Monangai’s status. That said, the consequences of his practice status are significant, particularly two days before a matchup with the reigning AFC champions who happen to be on a three-game winning streak.

Monangai tallied a total of 60 carries for 324 yards (5.4 yards per attempt) and three scores across the first four games of the season, which ranked him well within the top 10 rushing leaders in the NFL to that point. He added five receptions for 39 yards.

In the two games since Monangai went down, the Bears’ rushing totals fell alongside him. Chicago tallied 24 carries for 81 yards and one TD in Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers. The Bears then ran the football 33 times for 98 yards and three scores against the Atlanta Falcons last weekend.

Whether Monangai can play or not may well dictate how frequently — not to mention how effectively — Chicago’s offense can move the football on the ground against New England and subsequently control time of possession, which has long been an important element to head coach Ben Johnson’s offense.

Logic, Precedent Dictate Kyle Monangai Unlikely to Play for Bears Against Patriots on Thursday Night Football

Monangai did not practice at all in either of the past two weeks, which suggests his return on a short week is unlikely.

That is especially true because turf toe injuries are notorious for their potential to linger, and the Bears (4-2) will have 11 days off between their TNF game against the Patriots on Thursday and a Monday Night Football showdown on the road against the Seattle Seahawks on November 2.

Common logic and historical precedent point to the Bears holding Monangai out this week and revisiting his possible return ahead of their trip to Seattle. However, the contradictory reports out of Chicago on Tuesday have muddied the picture on Monangai’s status.

title: NFL reportedly will not punish Eagles for their handling of Jalen Hurts' blood clot
description:

text:
The Philadelphia Eagles received plenty of criticism after allowing quarterback Jalen Hurts to play in Week 5 despite knowing he was dealing with a blood clot in his calf. But after a review of the situation, the NFL reportedly does not feel that criticism was warranted.

The league reportedly found that the Eagles handled the situation "appropriately," per The Athletic. Because of that, the team will not face punishment for their approach with Hurts, who is now expected to miss the rest of the 2026 season after multiple blood clots were discovered in his lungs.

The Eagles came under fire Monday after revealing the full extent of Hurts' situation. In a joint statement, the team and Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, announced the quarterback was dealing with multiple blood clots in his lungs and would miss time while the issue was treated with blood thinners.

That news prompted some to reconsider Hurts' injury timeline and led to questions about the Eagles' approach to a very serious medical issue.

When Hurts took the field for the team's Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London, the Eagles knew the quarterback was dealing with a blood clot in his calf. Despite that, the team allowed Hurts to play in the game. It then allowed him to travel back to the United States to be evaluated later that week.

The Eagles placed Hurts on the injury report ahead of Week 5 with a calf injury, though they did not give him an injury designation for the contest. The NFL reportedly agreed that was the right call, per The Athletic, as Hurts' reps weren't expected to change despite the issue.

Hurts was able to practice without restriction Wednesday, but a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the blood clot, leading to the team ruling Hurts out for Week 6. In the team's statement announcing Hurts would miss Week 6, it said it was in constant communication with the NFL before Hurts played in Week 5.

Monday's statement, however, resulted in additional reports which painted the Eagles in a negative light. Tom Pelissero of The Ringer initially reported Monday that Hurts was advised by doctors to remain awake ahead of the London game as a precaution. Pelissero initially reported Hurts was awake for 36 straight hours before taking the field, leading to questions over whether the Eagles should have allowed the quarterback to play in that condition.

Later in the day, Pelissero walked back that report, saying Hurts was up until early Sunday morning, but was able to sleep ahead of the game. Additional reporting from The Athletic suggested Hurts was able to sleep from roughly 2:45 a.m. to 10 a.m. before the game. He also reportedly took a nap upon arriving at the stadium, per The Athletic.

When asked about the situation Monday, Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni declined to get into much detail, simply saying he relied on the medical experts who treated Hurts before allowing the quarterback to take the field in Week 5.

text:
It's been six weeks of hell for the Eagles this season and things seemingly can't get much worse for the 2-4 squad, right in the midst of a four-game losing streak. Their QB1 is out for the year due to blood clots in his lungs and several more of their Super Bowl winning roster is retired or in the infirmary.

Did the front office, led by Howie Roseman, make any logistical mistakes this past offseason? Or are most of their personnel issues simply bad luck?

Here's a quick whiparound as we look at how several key contributors from last season's NFC East title team are doing in new homes so far in the 2026 season:

Cam Jurgens, C, Ravens

The Eagles traded Jurgens for a second and fifth round pick, and so far, they're winning the trade. Jurgens has not been able to get himself out of the NFL's concussion protocol and has yet to make his Baltimore debut. We'll have to see if he's fully healthy and looking like his Pro Bowl caliber self when he finally gets on the field.

A.J. Brown, WR, Patriots

Eagles fans are probably feeling good about Brown as well. Jettisoned for a future first round pick this offseason, Brown was knocked out of his Patriots debut and onto the IR, where he missed five games. He returned last Sunday and had 10 targets. That's usually a recipe for Brown to do some real damage. But the former Eagles' All-Pro only caught three of those passes for 27 yards. Imagine if that had happened while he was in Philly.

Nakobe Dean, LB, Raiders

Do the Eagles miss their one-time stud linebacker? Dean has been healthy all year in Las Vegas, and leads all Raiders defenders with 56 tackles. He also has 1.5 sacks, four TFL and leads the NFL with three forced fumbles. This offseason the Eagles failed to match the three-year, $36 million the Raiders offered Dean, deciding they liked their LB depth. Zack Baun has been great when he's been healthy with Jeremiah Trotter Jr. and Jihaad Campbell splitting time at the other starter spot to mixed results.

Jaelan Phillips, DE, Panthers

Phillips had a half a sack last week against his former team, upping his season total to 2.5. He's dealt with hamstring issues all year and missed some playing time because of it, but the lackluster Eagles front four no doubt would be better with Phillips on the team. Was he worth the $120 million (over four years) Carolina threw his way? Roseman and company are confident he was not, instead trading two second round picks for Jonathan Greenard. Greenard has played in parts of three games and has zero sacks, and one total tackle.

Reed Blankenship, S, Texans

The former starting safety, who made the Eagles roster and won a Super Bowl as an undrafted free agent, has been up and down in his new digs in Houston. A few weeks ago against the Colts he had an interception and two passes defended, but since hasn't done much in coverage. He has a 108.0 QB rating against on 33 targets so far in 2026.

Sydney Brown, S, Falcons

Brown has played on about 36% of defensive snaps in Atlanta. He has a forced fumble and not much else on his stat sheet so far.

Za'Darius Smith, LB, Falcons

Smith, who retired briefly during his tenure with the Eagles due to serious personal issues, returned to the NFL and had a sack last week for the Falcons, giving him 3.5 for the season. He's been on the field for 94% of snaps this season.

A third straight Falcon, Dotson had a really solid showing in Week 6 against the Bears, catching three passes for 87 yards and a touchdown. He has more touchdowns (two) in six games with the Falcons than he had in 34 games with the Eagles.

He has 17 rushes for 43 yards so far in Carolina, where he's a backup to Chuba Hubbard.

The converted fullback is playing mostly on special teams for the undefeated Chiefs, where has five tackles.

The one-time depth pass rusher has found a solid home in Miami. Two weeks ago, Uche recovered a fumble. He also has a sack, playing on 67% of defensive snaps.

Patrick Johnson, DE, Raiders

The former Eagles draft pick has played on 24 total snaps on defense for Las Vegas this year.

The former depth tight end has the same role in Tennessee, where he's only seen action in two games.

Metchie had two catches for 24 yards against the Eagles last week. He has seven catches for 80 yards on the season.

Azeez Ojulari, DE, Raiders

Ojulari is on the Raiders practice squad.

Matt Pryor, OT, Patriots

Pryor was snagged from the Cardinals' practice squad by New England. He's since played in two games with the defending AFC champs.

Washington Commanders receiver Terry McLaurin is out for the remainder of the season with a torn left patellar tendon, coach Dan Quinn confirmed on Tuesday.

He will have surgery to repair the injury.

McLaurin, 31, suffered the injury on Monday against the 49ers and had to be carted off the field with an air cast on his left leg. He returned to the area and underwent an MRI to confirm the injury.

The eight-year veteran has played in five games so far this season and has 15 catches for 230 yards and a touchdown.

“Man, he brings a lot on and off the field," Quinn said. “I felt him in so many unique ways this season, from training camp to in-season. For him to even start the game like he did was significant.”

McLaurin and the Commanders agreed to a three-year deal worth $96 million just before the 2025 season, which put him under contract through the 2028 season. He is owed a $23.3 million salary in 2027 that includes $5.35 million that is guaranteed for injury if he isn’t healthy by April 1, which puts his future in Washington into question.

In his place, the Commanders will turn to Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams to produce more in the receiving game. Chig Okonkwo could also provide a spark at tight end.

Washington is 1-4-1 headed into its bye week after the 23-17 loss to the 49ers on Monday.

title: The Eagles must answer more questions about Jalen Hurts' blood clots - MS NOW
authors: Jarvis DeBerry, Kavitha A. Davidson, Allison Detzel, Anthony L. Fisher
description:
The Athletic reports that the NFL’s chief medical officer is defending the Eagles’ medical team.
But the failure to clarify the decision-making process around Hurts’ health has left the public with more questions than answers.
Who signed off on a transatlantic flight for a player with a blood clot, then only known to be in his calf?
There’s also business at stake here, though I can’t emphasize enough how irrelevant that is relative to Hurts’ health.
The NFL partners with sportsbooks that rely on accurate team injury reports as market information.
text:
UPDATE (October 20, 9:14 p.m. ET) The NFLPA released a statement Tuesday night calling for a “full investigation into what occurred” with Jalen Hurts. The Athletic reports that the NFL’s chief medical officer is defending the Eagles’ medical team.

After nearly two weeks of vague and contradictory statements about Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts’ health and a last-minute reversal on his injury status, the team announced Monday that its Super Bowl-winning captain has been diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in his lungs.

Hurts is now out indefinitely — at least for the rest of this football season. As dangerous as blood clots in the lungs are, his are considered treatable with blood thinners. But Hurts can’t participate in any football activities while receiving such medication, so it’s unclear when he might take the field again.

For a franchise that has won two championships in the past decade and has a front office with a reputation for doing things “the right way,” the lack of transparency surrounding Hurts has been jarring. While the team has long been cagey about what it says about players’ injuries, in this case, its lack of clarity has created a problem of public trust.

Head coach Nick Sirianni took questions from the media on Monday and said a whole lot of nothing, except that he has “full trust and full faith” in the team’s “medical experts.” We don’t know who that group of “medical experts” includes. The medical staff typically answers to the front office, but Eagles general manager Howie Roseman has been noticeably silent.

Hurts played a game in London against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Oct. 11 after it was determined he had a superficial blood clot in his left calf. Depending on the specifics, an athlete playing a contact sport with a blood clot can be deadly, but even though the sequence of events — and some apparent rumors — have provoked questions, there’s no evidence that the Eagles’ medical team did anything wrong. Certainly, teams must respect their players’ privacy. But the failure to clarify the decision-making process around Hurts’ health has left the public with more questions than answers. Everybody, including the players themselves and fans, should be able to count on teams doing right by their athletes, and the Eagles have yet to give the public that confidence.

Here’s the timeline as far as we know it: Hurts was cleated in the calf on Oct. 4 in the Eagles’ Week 4 loss to the Rams. Four days later, after being a full participant in practice, he sought treatment for that lingering calf pain. He then flew to London with the team ahead of its Week 5 matchup against Jacksonville.

The report that he was diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his left calf on Oct. 10 is per a joint statement from the team and Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn. According to initial reports from both NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Netflix’s Tom Pelissero, Hurts was advised by doctors not to sleep that night and remained at a London hospital until early morning on game day. Those initial reports that he had been awake 36 hours at kickoff have since been contradicted by his agent, who says he slept at Wembley Stadium before taking the field and throwing for 220 yards and a touchdown. He never appeared on the injury report with a game designation, which indicates whether an athlete is probable, questionable, doubtful or out.

Despite having already been diagnosed with a blood clot, Hurts took the transatlantic flight home and fully participated in practice for the Eagles’ upcoming home game against the Carolina Panthers. On Oct. 14, a follow-up ultrasound revealed that the clot had moved, and the next day, the Eagles ruled him out for the Panthers game. On Saturday morning before that game, ESPN reported that the team had “not even discussed the possibility of injured reserve” for Hurts, but the Eagles placed him on IR just a few hours later. Then came Monday’s announcement that Hurts had blood clots in his lungs.

That’s a bizarre timeline, and what we don’t know is striking. Who were the doctors who treated him in London and cleared him to play? Were they employed by the team? Were they independent specialists, or were they doctors from both camps? Who signed off on a transatlantic flight for a player with a blood clot, then only known to be in his calf? And why didn’t the team’s injury report reflect the diagnosis of his clot?

More articles

This is obviously bigger than football. A blood clot traveling to the lungs is a potentially fatal condition, and how a team handles the medical evaluation and clearance process can reflect and inform the actions of teams at every level of the sport, down to high school and youth leagues, where grind culture starts. Some commentators actually framed Hurts’ playing against Jacksonville as a sign of his “commitment to football” instead of questioning what information he had and what medical advice he received when the decision was made.

There’s also business at stake here, though I can’t emphasize enough how irrelevant that is relative to Hurts’ health. The NFL partners with sportsbooks that rely on accurate team injury reports as market information. The league should care most about its players’ health, but one might also expect it to care about the implications of the Eagles’ secrecy on people betting on games. Even so, The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones reports that “the NFL will not issue any punishment to the Eagles for its handling of the medical process, or for Hurts not being given an injury designation ahead of the game.”

In other words, the league has already looked into this and decided behind closed doors that everything’s just fine. We don’t know who the league spoke to, what information it reviewed or how it concluded that a player diagnosed with a blood clot could play without any designation and be allowed on a plane. We also have yet to hear from the NFL Players Association. If there were ever a moment for the union to be demanding answers, this would be it.

There’s precedent for a threat to a player’s health provoking change. In 2022, Miami Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa was seen stumbling after taking a hit and was still allowed to play. He suffered an even more frightening concussion four days later. Within two weeks, the NFLPA had dismissed the independent consultant who cleared him, and the league and union jointly changed the concussion protocol so that no one displaying Tagovailoa’s symptoms would be let onto the field. Notably, the review didn’t find that anyone had broken the rules, only that the outcome “was not what was intended” by the policy. And that’s the point: Nobody was found to be doing anything intentionally wrong, but the process ostensibly got better.

A similar investigation in warranted here. The next player in Hurts’ position deserves to know the system is working for him and not around him.

The Detroit Lions will have their first division game of the season this Sunday, hosting the 4-2 Green Bay Packers at Ford Field for a 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff.

Detroit got a head start on the week, moving their first practice from Wednesday to Tuesday, a common practice from this regime out of a bye week. Not only will Branch and Mays make their 2026 debuts for the team, but Detroit’s Tuesday practice had every single player on the active roster practicing. That includes the return of reserve cornerback Rock Ya-Sin, who had missed last game with a hamstring injury.

Now, it wouldn’t be completely accurate to call the Lions “fully healthy” at this point in the season. Another layer has been added to the Jalen Hurts situation, as the NFL Players Association released a statement Tuesday night calling for a full investigation by the league.

"The NFLPA is not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts. In fact, the league previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received.

Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."

Hurts is sidelined for the foreseeable future due to a deep vein thrombosis and several blood clots in his lungs. His last game was on Oct. 11, when the Philadelphia Eagles lost to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.

Details on the timeline of events and exactly what Hurts and the team knew have been disputed. At one point, the report was that the quarterback was told to stay awake for 36 hours before taking the field because of his injury. This was later walked back and clarified: he stayed awake but was given a space at the stadium to sleep.

It was reported earlier Tuesday that the NFL would not punish the Eagles, finding that the team handled the situation "appropriately," according to The Athletic.

Hurts appeared on the Eagles' injury report in Week 5 after a calf injury. It was later reported the Eagles knew he was dealing with a blood clot in his calf, but still allowed him to play. The team also let him travel back to the United States.

Philadelphia's statement in Week 5 said it was in constant communication with the league about the quarterback's status, injury and updates leading up to the game.

Last week, the quarterback underwent further testing, and an ultrasound revealed the blood clot had moved, and he was ruled out for Week 6. Even further testing this week showed there were multiple blood clots in his lungs, including a deep vein thrombosis and multiple pulmonary emboli.

text:
The NFL on Tuesday publicly and unequivocally defended how the Philadelphia Eagles managed the health of star quarterback Jalen Hurts after ultrasounds revealed blood clots had traveled to his lungs.

Hurts had been initially diagnosed with a superficial blood clot in his leg ahead of the Eagles’ game in London. He played every offensive snap of that game and flew back to Philadelphia, where he was subsequently diagnosed with bilateral pulmonary emboli and deep vein thrombosis and placed on blood thinners that will likely necessitate sitting out the remainder of the season.

On Monday, after the team and Hurts’ agent shared a joint statement detailing the diagnosis, critics questioned the decision to allow Hurts to play in the London game and take a transatlantic flight after a blood clot was discovered.

Throughout a 30-minute press conference on Tuesday at the NFL meetings in New York, Dr. Allen Sills, the NFL’s chief medical officer, repeatedly expressed his “tremendous confidence in the Philadelphia Eagles medical staff and all of our medical staff,” as well as the doctors at the Cleveland Clinic in London.

NFL executive vice president Jeff Miller rebuked what he called “considerable and uninformed speculation” which, on Monday, included reports that Hurts had not slept for 36 hours prior to the team’s game in London. The Eagles, like many teams playing abroad, had conversations with their players about the best way to handle the time difference between Philadelphia and London.

Sills pushed back on the implication that football factored into the medical care Hurts received while in London.

“Any idea or any suggestion that a team physician is ever being influenced by a coach, a general manager, a team owner, it just doesn’t happen,” he said.

However, several times he referenced the “shared decision-making” that doctors engage in with patients, seeming to imply that Hurts was an active participant of the process that led to him participating in the London game. He cited privacy concerns in declining to discuss Hurts’ situation specifically and resisted any sweeping hypothetical reviews of blood clot prognoses and procedures more broadly, citing the nuances of individual cases.

“We don’t have a protocol about this,” Sills said, contrasting it with established guidelines for issues like concussions.

The league does track blood clots and shares with the NFL Players Association.

“I don’t think you can take that outcome and say there was something flawed about the process,” Sills said. “Sometimes in medicine, we do all the right things and diseases progress and other things develop. I would look at the opposite side of that and say, in this case, everyone was incredibly conservative and incredibly vigilant and was very quick to make diagnoses of these conditions that might not have been diagnosed in a non-athlete.”

Asked specifically by CNN Sports whether the NFL conducted an investigation into exactly what did happen or whether they were simply confident that the Eagles’ staff did what should have, Miller said, “Both talking to the Eagles’ staff and making sure from people on the ground, tracking the case, talking to the independent hospital and doctors involved that we have, I think, a complete understanding of the course of events.”

On Tuesday night, however, the NFLPA put out a statement saying: “The NFLPA is not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts. In fact, the league previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received.

“Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward.”

The Los Angeles Rams are reportedly signing veteran kicker Brandon McManus in the wake of a season-ending injury to Blake Grupe, per NFL insider Ian Rapoport.

Grupe suffered a torn ACL in Sunday's loss to the Arizona Cardinals, per head coach Sean McVay. It was his first game with the team after signing following the release of Harrison Mevis, who missed two field goals in Week 5's loss to the Buffalo Bills.

Grupe made his first field-goal attempt with the team in the first quarter, but on the ensuing kickoff, he went for a tackle. Grupe didn't make the tackle and was sent flying, sustaining a knee injury.

The kicker was ruled out for the remainder of the game. In the fourth quarter, the Rams attempted an extra point, and punter Ethan Evans kicked it through the uprights. Earlier in the second quarter, L.A. went for two after scoring the touchdown, presumably because they were without their kicker.

text:
The Washington Commanders learned Tuesday that veteran receiver Terry McLaurin suffered a torn patellar tendon in his left knee during Monday night's 23–17 loss to San Francisco. McLaurin, 31, had to be carted off the field after suffering a non-contact injury in which he fell to the field and clutched his left knee. Dan Quinn spoke about it at his press conference Tuesday: "He'll get surgery, and he's going to miss the rest of the season. So I had a chance to speak with him last night on the plane and again after testing today," Quinn said. "Man, I'm gutted for him as a captain and one of our real leaders. So we're all here to support him. That was certainly tough news."

What NFL History Says About Patellar Tendon Tears

Looking ahead, NFL history shows us a median return timeline of around 11.4 months, according to a 2025 study in the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine that examined patellar tendon and quadriceps tendon injuries among NFL players. The study identified 45 NFL players with patellar tendon tears; 26 of them returned to play at least one game (57.8% return rate). The middle 50% of return times ranged from approximately 9.7 to 12.6 months.

Two solid, but different examples of players who returned from injury are former New York Giants WR Victor Cruz and former Saints/Seahawks TE Jimmy Graham. Both had the injury; both had different timelines to return. Cruz tore his patellar tendon on October 12, 2014, against Philly, but also had a completely separate calf injury during his return that led to him missing the entire 2015 season. In September of 2016, he finally returned after 700 days and caught a touchdown in his return. Graham tore his on November 29, 2015, had surgery, and returned for the 2016 season. He did miss a lot of training camp and all of preseason, but by November 2016, Graham was producing at a high level again, including an eight-catch, 103-yard, two-touchdown performance against Buffalo.

If your brain is already doing forward math, the study's median time to return to play was 11.4 months for those who returned, which would put McLaurin sometime around early October 2027. It is important to note: no timeline has been set for Terry McLaurin, and returning to practice, being cleared for contact, and playing in an NFL game are all different checkpoints.

With McLaurin, a team captain and face of the franchise for several years, gone for the season, the team will now need more from Stefon Diggs and the other receivers on the roster. Quinn talked a bit about the depth at his presser Tuesday: "I felt him in so many unique ways this season, from training camp to in-season. For him to even start the game like he did, I thought was significant. So we do have a deep crew at that position, and we'll lean in on a number of the guys to find some of the unique roles that Terry does." McLaurin's contested catch ability is something the team will miss. Quinn acknowledged that, "Terry's superpower is really on the contested catches, and that's one of the things that makes him excellent. But it's a big hit, and we'll lean on a number of guys."

Commanders receiver Terry McLaurin out for season with knee injury

Associated PressOctober 20, 2026 - 3:43pm

Washington Commanders receiver Terry McLaurin is out for the remainder of the season with a torn left patellar tendon, coach Dan Quinn confirmed on Tuesday.

He will have surgery to repair the injury.

McLaurin, 31, suffered the injury on Monday against the 49ers and had to be carted off the field with an air cast on his left leg. He returned to the area and underwent an MRI to confirm the injury.

The eight-year veteran has played in five games so far this season and has 15 catches for 230 yards and a touchdown.

“Man, he brings a lot on and off the field," Quinn said. “I felt him in so many unique ways this season from training camp to in-season. For him to even start the game like he did was significant.”

McLaurin and the Commanders agreed to a three-year deal worth $96 million just before the 2025 season, which put him under contract through the 2028 season. He is owed a $23.3 million salary in 2027 that includes $5.35 million that is guaranteed for injury if he isn’t healthy by April 1, which puts his future in Washington into question.

In his place, the Commanders will turn to Stefon Diggs and rookie Antonio Williams to produce more in the receiving game. Chig Okonkwo could also provide a spark at tight end.

Washington is 1-4-1 headed into its bye week after the 23-17 loss to the 49ers on Monday.

Lohner is likely still a few weeks away from a potential return. Crum will be one to watch this week because he's a valuable swing tackle. text:
The NFL ruled that the Eagles handled Jalen Hurts’ developing medical situation involving blood clots “appropriately” that ended his season and will not punish the team, according to The Athletic.

Hurts played in the Oct. 11 loss to the Jaguars in London without an injury designation despite the reveal of a blood clot in his left calf, although he had been flagged on the report with a calf injury.

The quarterback since has landed on injured reserve and reportedly will be sidelined at least three months after further testing revealed blood clots on his lungs.

The NFL communicated with the Eagles and their medical staff regarding the situation and ultimately determined the team did not violate league policies on injury report designation.

Hurts’ scary medical situation came to light last Thursday when the team announced he would miss the home game against the Panthers due to a blood clot in his left calf.

The team’s statement said Hurts requested treatment on his calf on Oct. 8, four days after being cleated during the Oct. 4 home loss to the Rams.

He received treatment that Friday, practiced in full and was added to the injury report, although he did not receive an injury designation since the team expected to play his full snaps allotment.

Hurts then underwent an ultrasound that Saturday before the Jaguars clash that revealed a superficial blood clot.

Allen Sills, the NFL’s chief medical doctor, worked with the EPL’s chief medical offer, Mark Gillett, to have Hurts examined at the Cleveland Clinic in London, per The Athletic.

Team and London doctors ruled that “activity and mobility were important” and he could “safely play.”

“The league had been in contact throughout the process with the Eagles medical personnel, and the Cleveland Clinic in London where the tests were conducted,” the NFL said in a statement to The Post, per a spokesperson. “The league’s Chief Medical Officer Dr. Allen Sills arranges for medical resources with leading providers in every international market with approval from the NFL Players Association.

“Medical care for players is provided by club medical staff in coordination with independent doctors.”

Hurts reportedly returned from the hospital around 2:45 a.m. and slept for roughly seven hours before starting the 19-17 loss.

“The health of our players is always at the forefront of our minds, and we leave that up to the medical experts, but we always, always care deeply about our players,” Eagles coach Nick Sirianni said about Hurts playing. “When you are completely focused on togetherness and connection, you’re always thinking about the well-being of your guys, and that’s where we were in that situation.”

Two days later, the team placed Hurts on injured reserve, sidelining him for a minimum of four games.

title: Jalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle? | Philadelphia Eagles
description:
Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the NFL season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs.
The quarterback complained to the Eagles’ medical staff of calf pain on 8 October, according to ESPN.
Asked about his decision to play Hurts, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni told reporters that he relies on advice from medical staff.
A study published this year found that 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players donated for research showed signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease that can only be diagnosed after death.
Last Wednesday, Hurts told reporters that his last week had been a “very unique experience” but declined to reveal the blood clot.
text:
Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the NFL season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. Thankfully, he’s now restricted from playing for the immediate future, meaning he won’t be risking serious complications – or even his life – as he did when he played in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.

The quarterback complained to the Eagles’ medical staff of calf pain on 8 October, according to ESPN. The Eagles say Hurts flew to London with the rest of the team and, out of an “abundance of caution”, was given an ultrasound. The test found a superficial clot in his calf. Doing an ultrasound before the flight would’ve been the most prudent thing. The same for making him inactive after the clot was found. But instead, he played in the game on 11 October, as the medical staff and doctors in London agreed “that activity and mobility were important”. Hurts also practiced all last week before a follow-up ultrasound also found clots in his lungs.

Some have celebrated Hurts’s performance against the Jaguars as a feat of virility; to many it looks more like putting a player in real danger. His blood clots could have caused serious health issues during the flights or game. (One sports medicine doctor told NJ.com that Hurts was “a walking risk”.) If his condition was dire enough that doctors reportedly told him in the early hours of Sunday morning not to sleep before the Jaguars game, he shouldn’t have been playing. Hurts’s agent, Nicole Lynn, clarified that he did get some sleep before facing the Jaguars, but the question remains: was the NFL’s London showcase so important that it was worth risking Hurts’s life?

Asked about his decision to play Hurts, Eagles coach Nick Sirianni told reporters that he relies on advice from medical staff. “I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation,” he said. “I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them as well.”

The Super Bowl LIX MVP is on blood thinners and hopefully on the road to healing, expected to make a full recovery. But his ordeal is the latest example of how football players are put in danger season after season. One piece of research from 2017 found that a college player took hits to his head during a single game that were equivalent to multiple car crashes. A study published this year found that 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players donated for research showed signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease that can only be diagnosed after death. The NFL has said that it “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts” but players keep on suffering concussions, and others like Hurts find themselves in a football culture where playing through injury is commonplace.

Last Wednesday, Hurts told reporters that his last week had been a “very unique experience” but declined to reveal the blood clot. No one has reported that he received any undue pressure from the Eagles or the league to play against the Jaguars. But it wouldn’t be shocking; this isn’t even the Eagles’ first controversial injury in London. In 2018, former Eagles tackle Lane Johnson was reportedly “berated” by general manager Howie Roseman for saying he was unsure about playing because of a high ankle sprain. After suiting up, Roseman reportedly told him, “Good, you have your mouthpiece in, now you can’t say anything stupid.” Neither man has commented on the matter, but it appears to offer a glimpse of life in the good ol’ NFL, where admitting you’re impaired is stupidity. Johnson aggravated the ankle injury and suffered a knee injury during the game.

Football culture demands players “tough it out” and get on the field. As former NFL receiver Bernard Berrian has said, the tension “isn’t verbal” but is still “there” because, “as we say, you can’t make the team in the training room.” Former running back Clinton Portis echoed Berrian when he spoke about playing through 10 concussions in his career and rarely getting treatment: “You can’t make the club in the tub.” Portis said he was “really scared” of undergoing testing to assess his neurological health.

You can see how the culture of the NFL makes players behave this way. With only 61% of NFL contracts containing guarantees, and an average 56% year-to-year retention, the pressure to stay active and keep the checks coming in is rampant. Pretty much every job pressures its employees to perform in some capacity; only one entails 300lb men running full speed to tackle you for 17 games a season. Players shouldn’t be made to feel they need to be on the field, but the irrational “win now” pressure they face trickles down and paints them in two colors: as an asset or expendable. It’s inherently inhumane.

The NFL has attempted to address injuries, and the threat of concussion and CTE in particular, but those efforts don’t seem to be enough. The league has changed kickoff rules and introduced oversized Guardian Caps to mitigate concussions, but football’s physical risks persist. A 2018 study in the Brain Neurology Journal revealed that subconcussive hits also contribute to CTE. And a 2025 Wisconsin School of Medicine study concluded that Guardian Caps did not reduce concussion rates in a sample of high school players. It’s unclear what seismic changes could actually address football’s inherent brutality. And the NFL’s struggles to stop it shows it is unsure – or doesn’t care enough – too.

Hurts’s case also raises the specter of medical racism. Multiple studies have shown that Black people and other minorities in the United States are less likely to receive adequate medical care than white people. It’s impossible to say whether the staff who treated Hurts looked at a strapping Black athlete and believed he could play a brutal game while suffering from blood clots. But the incident nonetheless conjures historical patterns and lived experiences of Black people not receiving proper care.

text:
The Philadelphia Eagles are not being punished for how they handled quarterback Jalen Hurts’ blood clots, according to the Associated Press. The league determined the Eagles did not violate its injury report policy, according to the report.

In a statement released Tuesday, the NFL said officials had been in contact with Eagles medical personnel and the Cleveland Clinic in London throughout the process of Hurts being treated.

The NFL said it stayed in contact with Eagles medical staff and Cleveland Clinic London during Hurts’ treatment. The league also said its chief medical officer helps arrange medical resources in international markets and that team doctors coordinate care with independent physicians.

Timeline: Hurts’ medical treatment

Hurts injured his left calf when he was hit by a cleat during the Eagles’ Oct. 4 game against the Los Angeles Rams. He sought treatment Oct. 8 and was listed with a calf injury the next day.

An ultrasound in London on Oct. 10 found a blood clot in his calf. The Eagles’ medical staff and doctors in London cleared him to play against Jacksonville after reviewing the results and recommending a follow-up scan within 72 hours. Hurts played in the Oct. 11 game, throwing for 220 yards and a touchdown in a 19-17 loss.

A follow-up ultrasound on Oct. 14 showed movement in the clot. The Eagles ruled Hurts out for their Oct. 18 game against Carolina and placed him on injured reserve the day before.

The Eagles and Hurts’ agent, Nicole Lynn, announced Oct. 19 that he had deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning blood clots had reached both lungs. Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season, sources told ESPN and NFL Network.

Lynn said Hurts’ prognosis is very good and that he is expected to make a full recovery. He is being treated with blood thinners and will not take part in football activities until he is off the medication. The team has not announced a timeline for his return.

The Houston Texans wide receiver room suddenly looks crowded, with Tank Dell set to play for the first time since 2024 when he suits up on Sunday against the New York Giants.

“I expect Tank just to be himself and just play the offense the right way,” coach DeMeco Ryans said on Monday, via the team’s official transcript. “No huge expectations from what he needs to do. We're all just going to be excited. I know me personally, I'm just going to be excited to see him just out there for the first time in over two years, just getting some game action. I'm just thankful, grateful for him to have this opportunity to return. I don't have any expectations. I'm just happy to see him out there and that's the only thing that matters.”

Sunday will mark Dell’s first game since Dec. 21, 2024, when he suffered multiple torn ligaments and a dislocated kneecap in the Texans' loss to Kansas City. The 2023 third-round pick sat out all of 2025 due to the injury.

The Texans slowly ramped up Dell’s practice work in previous weeks, wary of overloading him too soon after missing so much time. Returning for a smattering of reps before a Week 8 bye gives Houston a chance to ease him into the rotation in his first game in more than 670 days.

Ryans knows the shifty wideout will add a different element to the Texans' passing attack.

“As we all know, Tank is an explosive player,” he said. “He's still quick as ever. As our defenders who was covering him the past couple weeks, he's been putting us in some tough matchups and practice the past two weeks. I expect him to go out on Sunday and do the same thing. Really stress defenders and that's what Tank is going to do with his speed, his playmaking ability. He's going to stress defenders and you add them in a mix with all of the other guys that we have. We just have a really good group of guys, a lot of guys who are capable of making big time explosive plays for us.”

The Texans receiver room is suddenly crowded. Nico Collins is healthy and remains a go-to target as a big-bodied matchup nightmare for opponents. Second-year receiver Jaylin Noel is coming off the best game of his career (first 100-yarder). Houston traded for Marvin Harrison Jr., who, despite running just eight routes, was targeted four times in his first game (three catches, 34 yards). Kayshon Boutteremains a veteran threat. Xavier Hutchinson provides depth.

Now Dell returns to round out the group.

Ryans believes the unit’s interchangeability will make the offense harder for defenses to contain.

“Those guys can move around to a lot of different spots,” he said. “No one is just stuck in one particular position. Our coaches do a great job of moving them around. Everybody is versatile. We have a lot of different plays for different guys. We try to get as many guys touches as possible. That allows [Offensive Coordinator] Coach [Nick] Caley to mix it up really well with his play calls and set guys up to get opportunities to get the football ...

“Another thing I'm proud of with our receivers, is they do a great job of the contested catches. Marvin getting his first catch with us yesterday. The first one was a tough, contested catch over the middle. I just like how our guys are playing tough, as well as getting the explosive plays.”

Starting the season at 2-4, things are looking up for Houston, with tilts against the Giants, Chargers, Browns, and Colts on tap.

Terry McLaurin's season is over.
McLaurin suffered a torn patellar tendon in the Washington Commanders' 23-17 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Monday night, head coach Dan Quinn announced.

text:
Terry McLaurin's season is over.

McLaurin suffered a torn patellar tendon in the Washington Commanders' 23-17 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Monday night, head coach Dan Quinn announced. As a result, he will miss the rest of the season.

"I had a chance to speak to him last night on the plane, and again after testing today," Quinn said. "I'm gutted for him."

McLaurin was running a route near the end of the first quarter of Monday's matchup at Levi's Stadium when he suddenly fell near the sideline. Replay showed that McLaurin's left knee gave out on him and buckled as he was planting to the outside.

He remained down on the field for quite some time in front of the Commanders' bench, clearly in pain. A cart eventually came out for him. He hopped up into the back of the vehicle under his own power with his entire left leg in a full air cast, and players from both teams saw him off.

The Commanders quickly ruled him out with a knee injury, and Quinn said after the game that they feared the injury was significant. Now, after an MRI on Tuesday, McLaurin will have to undergo season-ending surgery.

McLaurin had one catch for 27 yards before he went down on Monday night. He'll finish the season, his eighth in the league with the Commanders, with 230 receiving yards and one touchdown.

The injury comes at a tough time for the Commanders. They fell to 1-4-1 on the season after Monday's loss in Santa Clara, which has them last in the NFC East. Though the division is still wide open — remarkably, nobody from the division has won a game in the past two weeks — losing a target like McLaurin is going to make things much more difficult for quarterback Jayden Daniels the rest of the way.

The Commanders are off in Week 7, and will return to take on the Philadelphia Eagles on Nov. 1.

title: Reports: NFL won't punish Eagles for letting Jalen Hurts play with blood clot - ESPN
authors: Tim McManus, Kalan Hooks, NFL Nation, Bill Barnwell, Ben Solak, Stephen Holder, Jordan Raanan, Daniel Oyefusi, Cameron Wolfe, Jamison Hensley
description:
PHILADELPHIA -- The NFL will not punish the Philadelphia Eagles for how they handled the process surrounding quarterback Jalen Hurts being cleared to play Week 5 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, according to multiple reports.

Hurts was initially diagnosed with what was described as a superficial blood clot in his calf.
Hurts' clot is considered to be "provoked" -- meaning a favorable prognosis with treatment and care -- because he was cleated in his calf, sources told Rapoport.
An ultrasound in London on Oct. 10 revealed Hurts' superficial blood clot.
text:
PHILADELPHIA -- The NFL will not punish the Philadelphia Eagles for how they handled the process surrounding quarterback Jalen Hurts being cleared to play Week 5 against the Jacksonville Jaguars, according to multiple reports.

The league's decision was first reported Tuesday by The Athletic, which also reported that the NFL determined the Eagles did not violate the league's injury report policy.

Hurts, 28, is expected to miss the rest of the season after doctors discovered multiple blood clots in the quarterback's lungs, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and ESPN's Adam Schefter on Monday.

In a statement released Tuesday, the NFL said officials had been in contact with Eagles medical personnel and Cleveland Clinic London throughout the process of Hurts being treated.

"The league's Chief Medical Officer, Dr. Allen Sills, arranges for medical resources with leading providers in every international market with approval from the NFL Players Association," the league said. "Medical care for players is provided by club medical staff in coordination with independent doctors."

Sills and other officials are expected to address reporters at the league's annual fall meeting later Tuesday in New York.

Hurts will undergo treatment involving blood thinners that is expected to sideline the three-time Pro Bowler for at least three months, sources informed of the diagnosis told Rapoport and Schefter.

Hurts' agent, Nicole Lynn, and the Eagles released a statement Monday detailing Hurts' condition. Lynn and the Eagles said Hurts has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, meaning a blood clot traveled from his legs to his lungs.

Hurts was initially diagnosed with what was described as a superficial blood clot in his calf. That diagnosis occurred in London before the Eagles' Week 5 game against the Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. Hurts played in that game -- a 19-17 loss for the Eagles -- despite the initial diagnosis and attempted 40 passes.

Sources told Rapoport that Hurts was in the hospital late at night in London and upon returning to the hotel at 3 a.m. local time, he was able to sleep until the team left for the stadium at 10:30 a.m. Upon arrival, Hurts napped until heading out to the field for pregame warmups.

Eagles coach Nick Sirianni did not go into detail about why Hurts was allowed to play in the Jaguars game after he was diagnosed with a blood clot but maintained that "the health of our players is always at the forefront of our mind" while expressing "full faith" in the team's medical experts.

"The same doctors and trainers that helped 21 of our 22 starters be available in the Super Bowl are the same guys today that deeply care about our guys, to help them," Sirianni said Monday.

Hurts' clot is considered to be "provoked" -- meaning a favorable prognosis with treatment and care -- because he was cleated in his calf, sources told Rapoport.

The Eagles placed Hurts on injured reserve three days ago after consultations with numerous doctors and experts. Hurts already had been ruled out for Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers, but the Eagles waited to make the roster move until after consulting with medical experts.

Sirianni would not reveal the contents of his personal conversations with Hurts but acknowledged that not having Hurts on the field for the foreseeable future will mean a transition.

"I haven't been without Jalen for an extended period of time," the coach said. "I have the utmost confidence in Tanner, but I miss him. I miss him, and I know that will be the case because Jalen and I have been together, head coach and quarterback, for six years, so that's natural."

"I don't want to speak for him in any sense of the matter, but I deeply care about him and hope that he continues to improve with what he's going through."

Hurts took a cleat to his calf area Oct. 4 against the Los Angeles Rams. He informed the Eagles' medical staff of the injury after practice Oct. 8 and was back at practice the next day before the team left for London.

An ultrasound in London on Oct. 10 revealed Hurts' superficial blood clot. The Eagles said last week that their medical staff and London-based doctors reviewed the ultrasound results and "concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play" against the Jaguars.

After returning to Philadelphia, Hurts underwent a follow-up ultrasound last Wednesday that revealed movement in the blood clot, prompting the Eagles to rule him out for the game against the Panthers.

Hurts hadn't missed more than two games in a season since becoming Philadelphia's quarterback in 2021. He is the fourth-leading passer in franchise history and has led the Eagles to three NFC East titles, two Super Bowl appearances and a victory over the Kansas City Chiefs two years ago in Super Bowl LIX, when he was named MVP.

text:
The San Francisco 49ers can breathe a sigh of relief knowing Mike Evans' injury status.

Evans played in his third consecutive game while dealing with injuries, but in the Week 6 matchup against the Washington Commanders, he was also battling Achilles soreness on top of his broken ribs.

He made three catches for 94 yards before limping off in the first half. San Francisco was up 23-3 before the threat of almost losing the game. He was so influential that the 49ers nearly picked up their first loss of the season.

Unlike when George Kittle tore his Achilles, it was evident in that matchup when he went down and was carted off. Evans walked back to the locker room after receiving a questionable-to-return designation, then was ruled out.

That looked somewhat positive, given how nasty and gruesome Achilles injuries are. Head coach Kyle Shanahan provided positive news on Evans after the 23-17 victory.

"It's something that he's had before," Shanahan said. "It's something that bothered him throughout the week. So, when you have Achilles tendonitis like he does, it kind of is what it is. It flared up tonight, and I hope he recovers throughout the week, but you don't think it's a long-term thing.

"But right now, it almost cost him this game and ended up costing him two quarters. Hopefully, he'll be able to play next week, but if not, we'll have to have the rest of the group step up, and hopefully, get him healed up by after the bye week."

It's a short turnaround on the schedule with the 49ers traveling east to face the Atlanta Falcons, Raheem Morris' former employer.

Shanahan expressed that Evans' judgement on his injury will give an indication on whether he features for Week 7, just before the bye week.

"I mean, if he can play, Mike's got a lot of experience on doing this stuff. Mike's pretty honest with us, too, and my life experience is with him over six games. If he says he's ready to go, I believe him," said Shanahan.

It's the best news possible that Evans' injury isn't worse. He's made an exceptional impact since joining, plus the 49ers are thin at wide reciever.

text:
Washington Commanders receiver Terry McLaurin tore the patellar tendon in his left knee and will miss the remainder of the season, coach Dan Quinn said.

McLaurin suffered the injury late in the first quarter of Monday's 23-17 loss at San Francisco. The injury also calls into question his future with the Commanders.

"Man, he brings a lot on and off the field," Quinn said. "It's a big hit, and we'll lean on a number of guys."

McLaurin, 31, leads Washington with 230 yards receiving on 15 receptions. He finished with one catch for 27 yards Monday. But with two minutes, 16 seconds left in the opening quarter, McLaurin was injured while cutting on a route; the play ended with a sack of quarterback Jayden Daniels.

McLaurin also missed a Week 4 game against the Indianapolis Colts after injuring his hamstring two days before the game, but he returned a week later.

He sat out seven games in 2025, ending a streak of 72 consecutive games played. Before last season, he had been a consistent producer, with five consecutive 1,000-yard seasons, from 2020 to 2024.

He has been the emotional engine of Washington's offense since joining the team as a third-round pick in 2019. He also was named a captain for this season.

McLaurin became a fan favorite and a face for the franchise during a turbulent period that featured five losing seasons in his first seven years; multiple investigations into the franchise and former team owner Dan Snyder and a sale of the team.

McLaurin also played with 13 different starting quarterbacks until Daniels arrived in 2024. It was the first time he played with the same opening day starter in consecutive seasons.

But now McLaurin's future with Washington could be in jeopardy. He signed a three-year extension in 2025 after missing all of training camp during negotiations. The deal allowed Washington to either release him after the season or to restructure. Otherwise, he would count $34 million against the salary cap and $39.5 million in 2028.

If he is released, Washington would save approximately $8.5 million on the cap next year.

text:
Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce received a strong message from former teammate Gehrig Dieter after playing through an ankle injury during Sunday's 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers.

Kelce suffered the injury early in the October 18 matchup at Arrowhead Stadium after Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley tackled him. His leg appeared to get caught underneath the defender, and he limped toward the sideline.

The 37-year-old tight end received treatment from the Chiefs' medical staff, who wrapped his ankle before he returned to the field.

Kelce finished the game with four receptions for 53 yards as Kansas City improved to 5-0.

Dieter, a former Chiefs wide receiver who won a Super Bowl with Kelce, praised his former teammate for continuing to play despite the injury.

"Kelce is a dawg! They don't make 'em like him anymore," Dieter wrote on X. "Anyone else would be milking that ankle injury."

Former Chiefs Receiver Gehrig Dieter's Comments Spark Fan Reactions

Dieter's message drew responses from Chiefs fans who agreed with his assessment of Kelce's toughness.

One fan called the tight end a "beast," while another described him as the "GOAT."

Another fan suggested Kelce would be reluctant to miss time this season, no matter the circumstances.

"PREACH! This dude is gonna play unless he doesn't have a pulse this season," the fan wrote. "And we are all here for it!"

Dieter spent time with the Chiefs from 2017 through 2021 and was part of the team's Super Bowl LIV championship roster.

His comments came as Kelce continued his 14th NFL season, having already established himself as one of the league's most productive tight ends.

Before facing Los Angeles, Kelce had recorded 246 receiving yards and two touchdowns through Kansas City's first four games.

He also entered the matchup ranked second among NFL tight ends with a Pro Football Network TE Impact Score of 86.6.

Andy Reid Shares Update on Travis Kelce's Ankle After Chargers Game

After the win, Chiefs head coach Andy Reid addressed Kelce's injury and what it could mean going forward.

According to A to Z Sports reporter Charles Goldman, Reid said Kelce tweaked his ankle but still finished the game.

"Travis Kelce tweaked his ankle and played through it. Says he'll be sore tomorrow, but he'll be OK," Reid said, per Goldman.

Kelce also appeared to move without a noticeable limp as he entered the locker room after the game.

Sports Radio 810 shared footage showing the tight end smiling as he walked through the stadium.

Although Reid expects some soreness, his comments indicated that the team was not anticipating a serious issue.

The Chiefs entered the matchup already dealing with injuries to wide receivers Tyquan Thornton and Rashee Rice.

Several more players experienced injuries against Los Angeles.

According to reporter Pete Sweeney, Reid provided updates on offensive linemen Jaylon Moore and Kingsley Suamataia, along with wide receiver Jalen Royals.

"Chiefs head coach Andy Reid said Jaylon Moore has a concussion, Travis Kelce played through an ankle injury, Jalen Royals was checked for a concussion, but he was OK, and Kingsley Suamataia got kicked in the calf," Sweeney reported on X.

Moore's concussion adds another concern for Kansas City's offensive line, while Suamataia's calf injury will also require attention.

Washington Commanders @ San Francisco 49ers

Jacory Croskey-Merritt lands on injured reserve: Washington's leading rusher will miss at least four games with a groin injury.

Washington has relied on Croskey-Merritt as its early-down back and Rachaad White as its receiving back this season, with Austin Ekeler returning to the mix when White missed time. Ekeler entered this game less than 100% healthy after being limited in practice all week with a chest injury. The Commanders also activated Jeremy McNichols from injured reserve earlier in the day, eliminating the need to elevate Craig Reynolds from the practice squad, as they had earlier in the season. That left Washington with an interesting combination of three running backs who have each served as the team's third-down back at different points over the past three seasons.

White handled the bulk of the work tonight, with Ekeler occasionally rotating in and McNichols not seeing his first offensive snaps until the third quarter. While White dominated snaps, it's worth noting that Washington lost the time-of-possession battle, giving White several extended breaks without necessarily needing another back to spell him. Ekeler's lingering chest injury may have also contributed to the lopsided workload.

White can generally be considered a fantasy starter for the next three games based on his dominant share of the backfield snaps, although there's no guarantee the Commanders will maintain this rotation going forward.

Commanders adjust without Terry McLaurin: The Commanders briefly had their wide receiver room intact before another injury forced them to adjust.

Washington was without McLaurin (hamstring) in Week 4 and Stefon Diggs (hamstring) in Week 5. Both players, along with Treylon Burks (shoulder), were limited in practice at times this past week. While Jaylin Lane remains out for the season, this was the healthiest Washington's wide receiver room had looked in several weeks.

Washington opened with McLaurin as its lead receiver, Burks joining him in 12 personnel and Diggs and Antonio Williams joining him in 11 personnel. That alignment lasted just two drives before McLaurin left with a knee injury. He was carted to the locker room with an air cast on his leg and quickly ruled out, suggesting the injury could be serious.

Washington shifted to a heavy rotation of players in 12 and 13 personnel, while Burks, Williams and Diggs were the primary receivers in 11 personnel. Dyami Brown rotated in at times, while Luke McCaffrey saw his first offensive snaps of the season.

Burks was injured in the final two minutes while attempting to catch the game-winning touchdown. He wasn't available for Washington's final two-minute drive, when Brown, Williams and Diggs served as the three receivers. Burks would be a solid waiver-wire target going forward, but only if McLaurin's injury is as serious as it appeared and Burks' own injury isn't serious.

Chig Okonkwo has excellent route participation rates: Okonkwo was almost always running a route whenever the Commanders called a pass play.

Okonkwo was a popular sleeper tight end this offseason after the Commanders acquired him from the Tennessee Titans. He was off to a strong start in Week 1 in terms of playing time before suffering a hamstring injury that kept him out in Weeks 2 and 3. He was then eased back into action in Week 4.

Last week, his playing time increased to 71% of the snaps. He was almost always the tight end on the field in 11 personnel and played 91% of the snaps in 13 personnel, but was rarely on the field in 12 personnel. This week, he rotated out at times in 13 personnel, which wasn't a concern because those were mostly run plays. He also remained on the field for most plays out of 12 personnel. As a result, he ranked among the league leaders in route participation at tight end this week, joining Brock Bowers, Isaiah Likely, Trey McBride and George Kittle.

Okonkwo caught seven passes for 69 yards, leading the team in receiving yards. The Commanders have their bye week next week, but Okonkwo would be a strong option for anyone looking for a tight end who could potentially start for their fantasy team later in the season.

The 49ers adjust without all of their top receivers: Deebo Samuel Sr. was inactive for this game, while Mike Evans left before halftime.

San Francisco has used nine wide receivers this season. De’Zhaun Stribling and Demarcus Robinson have landed on injured reserve, while KhaDarel Hodge was released with an injury. Ricky Pearsall and Christian Kirk started the season on injured reserve, and Samuel didn't practice all week because of a hamstring injury before being ruled out Saturday.

This left Evans, Jacob Cowing, Jordan Watkins and Brandin Cooks as the available receivers on the 53-man roster, with Malik Turner elevated from the practice squad. Evans didn't practice all week because of rib and Achilles injuries and was questionable, but he was active.

San Francisco used a straightforward wide receiver rotation, with Evans as the X receiver, Watkins at Z and Cowing joining them in 11 personnel, often in the slot. Cooks backed up Evans, while Turner backed up Watkins. The 49ers typically kept their X receiver on the field in 22 personnel. Evans played 25 of the first 38 snaps before heading to the locker room just before halftime because his Achilles injury was bothering him. He was ruled out shortly after halftime, but not before catching three passes for 94 yards.

Cooks took over as the X receiver following Evans' departure. San Francisco faces the Atlanta Falcons next week, a favorable matchup for wide receivers, before heading into its bye week. If the 49ers decide to sit Evans next week to give him additional time to recover, Cooks would be the best waiver-wire pickup from this group, as he's in the strongest position to produce.

Miscellaneous Notes

With the injuries at wide receiver, San Francisco ran five plays with both Kaelon Black and Christian McCaffrey on the field, with McCaffrey lined up as a wide receiver. The 49ers hadn't used this personnel grouping at any point over the first five weeks.

San Francisco running back Kyle Juszczyk was back in the lineup after missing last week's game with a knee injury. He was limited in practice Thursday before being upgraded to a full participant Friday.

49ers wide receiver Christian Kirk returned to practice from injured reserve Thursday. He was limited in practice with a calf injury and was listed as questionable, but he remains on injured reserve.

Commanders quarterback Marcus Mariota didn't practice all week because of a knee injury and was ruled out Saturday, marking his second straight absence.

text:
The Vikings wrapped up their Week 5 matchup against the Saints with a win, but they were also down multiple starters with various injuries. However, last week's conveniently placed bye allowed many of them to get healthy ahead of a Week 7 date with the Colts.

Despite the win, the Vikings were without Jordan Addison, Christian Darrisaw and more against New Orleans. So, who could be back, and who might be out for some time yet?

Here is the latest on the Vikings' injuries coming out of the bye.

Vikings who could return in Week 7

Jordan Mason, RB

Mason was put on short-term IR after injuring his thumb in Week 1. Aaron Jones was left as a one-man wrecking crew and was an absolute workhorse in Mason's absence, notching 97 touches during the four-week recovery. But with Mason now on the mend, it looks like Jones may get a bit of a rest in Week 7.

ESPN's Kevin Seifert reported on Monday that the Vikings have activated Mason from IR and expect him back at Wednesday's practice ahead of their matchup against Indianapolis, although his potential workload is still unclear.

Jordan Addison, WR

Addison was close to suiting up against the Saints in Week 5, according to head coach Kevin O'Connell, so he should be a sure thing to play against the Colts this weekend after two weeks of recovery time. Addison had been nursing a hamstring injury and tested it pregame against New Orleans but couldn't get to 100%. He'll be very close to that number now.

Addison has just 11 catches this year and needs some big games moving forward to earn a huge extension this offseason.

T.J. Hockenson, TE

The Vikings lost Hockenson on the second play of their opening drive against New Orleans, and the tight end was placed into the concussion protocol after the game. Every injury is different, but he'll likely clear in time to suit up Sunday.

If he can't go, Minnesota will get another strong dose of Bartholomew, who racked up five catches in Hockenson's absence in Week 5.

Christian Darrisaw, LT

Darrisaw left the Miami game with a concussion and was put into the protocol. He had initially left the game with a neck injury before returning briefly, then left the contest for good after experiencing concussion symptoms. Darrisaw has had a bit more time to recover than Hockenson, so his status should be good for Week 7, but both will need to be fully cleared before taking the field.

This most recent missed game now assures that Darrisaw will go six straight seasons with at least one spent on the sidelines. As talented as he is, Darrisaw has never made it through a full 17-game season in his career.

Vikings who are out for the season

Both guard Donovan Jackson and tight end Josh Oliver are confirmed to be out for the year, with Jackson suffering a torn meniscus and Oliver a torn triceps. Joe Huber has filled in for Jackson, while the young duo of Gavin Bartholomew and Ben Yurosek have picked up the slack at tight end.

The Vikings also lost safety Jamal Adams before the season with a torn quadriceps, as well as edge rusher Tyler Batty with a torn ACL.

text:
Brock Purdy threw a touchdown pass, Christian McCaffrey ran for two scores and the San Francisco 49ers held on to beat the Washington Commanders 23-17 on Monday night for their sixth straight win to open the season.

The Niners followed up an emotional win last week at division rival Seattle by building a 20-point lead and holding off the Commanders (1-4-1) with two late defensive stops.

“[The defense] did it for us all game, I’m proud of those guys ... our defense balled,” Purdy said after the game.

Jayden Daniels threw two touchdown passes in the second half to cut that 20-point deficit to 23-17, but Malik Mustapha broke up a fourth-down pass to Treylon Burks near the goalline with 1:54 to play to preserve the lead.

Washington got the ball back at its 46 with 52 seconds remaining and moved down to the 28 before Daniels was called for intentional grounding, giving the Commanders one last play from the 40. Daniels was then sacked by Keion White and Ogbo Okoronkwo before he could throw up a desperation pass.

The Niners extended their best start of a season since winning their first eight games in 2019 on the way to a Super Bowl appearance.

Purdy started the game fast with a 24-yard strike to Mike Evans, who later left the game with an achilles injury, on the third play of the game and an 11-yard touchdown to George Kittle to finish that drive. Purdy went 21 for 29 for 264 yards and officially became the highest-rated quarterback in NFL history as he passed the 1,500-attempt threshold to qualify. His 105.6 rating is ahead of Lamar Jackson’s 102.7.

The Commanders were unable to bounce back from last week’s tie against the New York Giants, when they mismanaged the clock in overtime to cost them a chance at a game-winning field goal.

The game was one-sided early with the 49ers scoring touchdowns on the first two drives on Purdy’s pass to Kittle and a one-yard run by McCaffrey.

San Francisco expanded the lead to 20-3 late in the half on McCaffrey’s second touchdown run as the Niners gained as many first downs (17) in the first half as the Commanders ran plays.

The Commanders lost star receiver Terry McLaurin to what looked like a severe knee injury during the game, and he is likely to miss a significant amount of time.

“He’s a brother to me. It sucks,” Daniels said. “You see how hard he works ... Praying for Terry. He’s been there for me through a lot since I came into this league, the adverse times I went through last year and so far this year, and he’s been right by my side. I love Terry and appreciate him a lot.”

text:
The news that Philadelphia Eagles star Jalen Hurts has a likely season-ending injury of blood clots has sparked questions about how the condition developed in one of the NFL's top quarterbacks.

Hurts, 28, was diagnosed earlier this month with a superficial blood clot in his leg that then traveled to his lungs, developing into deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, the Eagles said Monday in a joint statement with Hurts' agent.

A diagnosis of bilateral pulmonary emboli -- meaning there are blood clots on both Hurts' right and left lungs -- can be serious, potentially causing permanent damage to the lung, low oxygen levels in the blood and damage to other organs in the body from not getting enough oxygen.

Hurts is currently on blood thinner medication, which prevents him from playing football, according to the Eagles. The team did not provide a timeline for Hurts' potential return to the field.

Here is a timeline of Hurts' injury, according to statements provided by the Eagles organization.

Timeline of Hurts' injury

Sunday, Oct. 4 -- Hurts is "cleated" during a game against the Los Angeles Rams in Philadelphia.

Wednesday, Oct. 7 -- Hurts practices in full with Eagles team.

Thursday, Oct. 8 -- Hurts practices in full with Eagles team. After practice, he informs the Eagles' medical staff that he was cleated during the Rams game and receives treatment for a calf injury.

Friday, Oct. 9 -- Hurts receives medical treatment and practices in full with the team.

Friday, Oct. 9 into Saturday, Oct. 10 -- Hurts flies to London with Eagles team.

Saturday, Oct. 10 -- Hurts undergoes an ultrasound that reveals a superficial blood clot.

Sunday, Oct. 11 -- Sources told ESPN that Hurts was hospitalized in London until 4 a.m. on Sunday. He then plays in the Eagles' 17-19 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Hurts and the team fly home immediately following the loss.

Monday, Oct. 12 -- Hurts receives medical treatment.

Tuesday, Oct. 13 -- Hurts receives medical treatment.

Wednesday, Oct. 14 -- Hurts practices in full with the team. A follow-up ultrasound done in the evening shows movement in the small blood clot.

Thursday, Oct. 15 -- Eagles announce Hurts will not play in Sunday's game against the Carolina Panthers.

Sunday, Oct. 18 -- Hurts is absent from the sidelines of the Eagles' loss to the Panthers.

Monday, Oct. 19 -- The Eagles and Hurts' agent announce the quarterback has deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli, and is taking blood thinner medication. As a result, he will be sidelined for an indefinite amount of time.

Deep vein thrombosis, or DVT, is when a blood clot develops in the deep veins, usually in the legs. A pulmonary embolism, or PE, occurs when a part of the DVT clot breaks off and travels to the lungs, which can be life-threatening, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
